utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning, everybody. Good morning, Witness. Would you please stand up and make the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would you please tell us what your name is.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: My name is Mico Gavric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: G-a-v-r-i-c.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Gavric, where are you from?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: The village of Opravdici, Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And where do you currently live?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: In Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would you please tell us a little bit about your background. Where did you go to school?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was born on the 15th of September, 1957, in the village of Opravdici, Bratunac municipality. I went to primary school in Kravica. I went to the secondary vocational mining and technical school in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Did you attend any further schooling after that?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: After I had graduated from the secondary vocational technical school, I went to do my military service. And I completed the school for reserve officers of the artillery department. Once I had returned from the army in 1979, I went back and got a job in the zinc and lead mine of Sase in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. This school for reserve officers, can you tell us a little bit about that. How long did it take and what was the focus of your studies?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: The school for reserve officers lasted seven months. It began on the 1st of September, 1978, and went on until the 30th of April, 1979.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So after you completed this school, you said you went back to work in the Sase mine. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: After I had completed school - and this school lasted for seven months - I did some practical training, that is to say I did my military service in the 3rd Guards' platoon -- regiment of Pozarevac, where I was an instructor, a teacher at the school for reserve officers of -- at republican level of the first army of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And for how long were you an instructor there?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I was there for six months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you returned to the Sase mine, what position did you hold there?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: After returning from my military service, I went back to the mine, the lead and zinc mine in Sase, in Srebrenica, where I was the leader or manager in the productions department. That is to say, I was shift supervisor in the lead and zinc mine for production.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you please tell us whether you were supervising any individuals, and if so, what was the number of people that you were supervising?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: As I said a moment ago, I was supervisor, which means that I was in charge of production in the mine, in the lead and zinc mine, where I had usually about 150 to 230 employees under me and my shift. And I was their immediate superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: For how long did you work at the Sase mine?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I worked there until 1990 when I left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And after you left, where did you work?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: After leaving the mine, I went to work in a private company, and it was my own company. I established it in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Where do you work today?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I work in the same company, as I did previously, but now there are more employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you said that's your company. Could you please tell us how many employees do you have.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: We have a permanent staff of 30 workers, and that is in season, in high season -- actually, in high season, if need be, we have 10 to 15 extra workers that we take on through the youth organisation, youth cooperative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, were you ever mobilised during the war?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please tell us when was it that you were mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: On the 17th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And could you please tell us when you were mobilised what functions, if any, did you have.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: When I was mobilised on the 17th of May, 1992, I reported to the TO command of Bratunac, and the commander of the TO of Bratunac I think, as far as I remember, was Mile Bozic, a major, or perhaps it was Momir Nikolic, a captain, as far as I remember at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you were mobilised, in light of your military service with the JNA and your schooling that you had, were you given any particular tasks?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. Since I was one of the superiors who had been trained for ground force artillery, I was given the assignment of forming and establishing the artillery units, or rather, that I was to make up a full complement for the command cadres and crews.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. During that period of time, could you briefly tell us what sort of equipment the TO had with respect to your particular unit.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the initial stage of establishment of the units of the Territorial Defence, the artillery group, as we used to call it at the time, had within its composition six mortars of 82-millimetre calibre; four mortars of 120-millimetre calibres, the M-52 type; two Howitzers of 105 millimetres; two cannons of the M31/37 type, manufactured in Russia; and four artillery pieces of the B-1, 105-millimetre calibre type -- I'm sorry, I meant 86-millimetre calibre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if you could just briefly list the Muslim offensives against the Serbs in that Bratunac area from the time you were mobilised until the time Srebrenica was declared an enclave.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'll do that. The first onslaught by the enemy forces was on the 29th of May, 1992, when they captured our combat vehicle, the DR9. At the time, we were led by Captain Momir Nikolic. On that day, we had a large number of wounded and killed. Then the following offensive by the Muslim forces was launched on the 9th of June, 1992. And that took place against the village of Obad, where I think there were between seven to ten civilian casualties, mostly elderly people, I mean elderly men. The following offensive launched by the Muslim forces was against Serb territory and Serb villages, and that was on the 5th of July, 1992, against the village of Zagoni, where there were 12 dead, mostly civilians, elderly, and small children. The next operation, or rather, attack launched by the Muslim forces from the direction of Srebrenica was an all-out attack against all the Serb villages in the surrounding parts, starting out from the village of Zagoni, and that was attacked on the 5th, and then we liberated it. After that came the village of Borici in Bratunac municipality. This was followed by Kunjerac, another village, and the waterworks there that supplied the town of Bratunac with its water supply. And then Rudnik, or rather, the mine, the zinc and lead mine of Sase and Srebrenica, followed by the village of Zalazi, where I think there were between 60 and 70 casualties. Of those 60 or 70 casualties, ten were taken alive, our soldiers were taken alive, and probably they were killed. And -- because today nobody knows where their graves are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about Serb attacks against the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: If you will allow me to complete what I was saying about the Muslim offensives, I will do so and then I will go back and give you the chronological order of the Serb offensives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Sorry to interrupt. Okay, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: After the 7th, or rather, the 12th of July, which was St. Peter's Day, Petrovdan, the following operation launched by the Muslim forces against Serb villages took place on the 8th or 9th of August, 1992. And it was against the village of Jezestica. I think that it was the 20th of August when the Magasici village was attacked, and in both these attacks they were mostly civilian casualties. In the first attack, which as I said was between the 8th and 9th against the village of Jezestica, someone, one of the Muslim fighters, cut off the head of one of our fighters who were putting up the village defence. And I know that that man's surname was Mladjenovic and his head was cut off. And in the village of Magasici on the 20th of August, in addition to the many casualties, there was a woman who was the wife of the priest, and she was between the ages of 20 and 21 and she was pregnant, she was expecting a baby, and her throat was slit. The next operation launched by the Muslim forces was -- took place at the beginning of September against the village of Takovici, or rather, the local commune there. It was in this area that they set fire to and killed everything they encountered on the way. They burnt down the primary school and the Orthodox church. The following operation launched by the Muslim forces took place on the 14th -- between the 14th and 15th of December, 1992. And that was against the village of Bjelovac. I think there were 109 casualties on that occasion. In the area, I know that many civilians were killed. I can also say that soldiers were killed as well; that's the truth. But amongst the civilians, unfortunately, I do know for a fact that an old lady was killed, and I know her, her name was Lavta [phoen]. I think she was 84 years old. Then there was a young girl and several other young girls who were killed, which confirms that they -- that they were not soldiers. The next operation launched by the Muslim forces took place on the 24th of December, 1992, against the village of Glogova. It was in this village that there -- the casualties were all soldiers, and there were 12 of them. And they were providing security for the Bratunac/Kravica road and communication line. The next operation launched by the Muslim forces was one that took place on the 7th of January, 1993, on the day of the Orthodox Christmas and -- just a moment, please, to collect myself. I apologise. Everything was destroyed. I am sorry for this, but it's my -- the area that I come from, so -- anyway, I think there are about 70 victims. And the final official onslaught in 1993 by the Muslim forces took place on the 16th of January. At that time it was a municipality, today it is the local community of Skelani. They killed everyone they came across, and at the border crossing itself on the bridge, they killed a certain number of people, too. I would like to say that those are all the Muslim offensives in the Bratunac area that I remember. And they were completed by the proclamation of -- when Srebrenica was proclaimed an enclave, that is to say by the 18th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, during this period, certainly you're not suggesting that the Serbs were not attacking the Muslims or launching counterattacks?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: In certain cases, when there were -- when a Serbian village was attacked, when the village of Jezestica in fact and the village of Magasici, and I'm taking them in order. So I'm starting on the 8th and 9th of August, and then I'm going on to the 20th of August. But I apologise, I have to go back to the 5th of July, the village of Zagoni, then we come to the 12th. So in all these Muslim operations, if I can put it that way, the Serb forces, wherever they had occasion to regain control of their territory and liberate the Serb villages and pull out the dead and wounded, they did so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I don't think those issues are related to the subject matter of this case. Could we move to the critical period as soon as possible?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We will be moving, though, Your Honour, if we look at the indictment, we look at paragraph 18 that talks about May 12th. And then we go on to paragraph 19, there's a total absence of any Muslim attacks against the Serbs. Then if you look at my pleadings, when I suggested to Judge Schomburg that additional facts needed to be included in the indictment for purposes of objectivity and fairness and perspective, Judge Schomburg denied my motion as being premature and indicated in my decision that I could bring these matters out during the trial. So I just wanted to briefly cover that period, but I take the Court's point and I will be moving on. But that was the reason why I wanted to get this historical context in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Sir, could you please tell us whether you served in the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And could you tell us about what time was the Bratunac Brigade formed, to your recollection.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Bratunac Brigade was formed on the 14th of November, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, could you please tell us in the Bratunac Brigade what position you held.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. Once the Bratunac Brigade was formed, I was appointed to the duty of head of the artillery of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So I take it you had the same -- more or less had the same position that you had when there was a Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: During my testimony, you will be able to see that from start to finish I was at that duty, at that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, could you please tell us when the Bratunac Brigade was formed, did the military equipment that you had when it was a Territorial Defence, did it increase at any point, your particular unit?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: My particular unit, as far as I remember, did not increase in terms of military equipment, nor did it decrease while the war operations were going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, if we could focus in July 1995 - and we're going to get there in great detail - but if you could just tell us the operational condition of the equipment that your unit had.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: The condition of the equipment that we had, or rather, our artillery pieces, it was in relatively good condition. All the shortcomings or problems that ensued we dealt with through putting in a request to the corps, or rather, the institute at Hadzici, Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, could you please tell us how many -- since you were the commander of this artillery unit, could you please tell us how many men were you supervising.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: If we look at the overall number of men and the command departments and crew and the physical security, computers, and so on, we had about 80 persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, in addition to or aside from your particular unit, did the battalions have their own artillery hardware that they would use?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you also -- they under you? Were you the superior officer for those units that were working within the battalions?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No. According to the rules, the infantry battalions, according to the establishment, had battalion fire groups, anti-tank groups, and according -- under their leadership were the platoons of 70 -- 60-, 82-, and 120-millimetres mortars or recoilless guns for anti-armour combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Who was your immediate, your immediate, commanding officer?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I was personally and directly subordinated to the brigade commander, because I belonged to the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to focus on July 1995, that period. And in particular, as a point of reference, I'm going to use July 11th as the day that Srebrenica fell. All right? Could you please tell us whether you participated in those events, the attack on Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And could you please tell us where your unit was located at the time.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: As the Bratunac Brigade was, for a long time throughout this period, on the defensive, our units and our artillery fire positions were located in the areas in the rear behind the front end of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you change your positions for the attack on Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No, because there was no need.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, first of all I want to go through some documents, and then we're going to get to it step by step. If I could have you look at P405, which has been admitted. So you have the Srpski version, which is P405B. Could you please look at that for a second. Now, before coming here today, have you seen this report?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And when -- where and when did you see it?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: This is the combat report of the Bratunac Brigade. I think I saw it in the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if you could look at number 2. Incidentally, what -- we see at the top of it, we see it's dated 4 July, 1995. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you look at paragraph number 2, it states here: "The brigade commander," the second sentence starts with: "The brigade commander is visiting the artillery firing positions and the chief of staff is visiting positions of the 2nd Battalion infantry -- the 2nd Infantry Battalion." Do you recall whether on that particular day, July 4, 1995, the brigade commander visited your firing positions?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: To be quite honest, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to show you the next document, which is P406. And again, your version would be 406/A. Do you recognise this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And what do you recognise it to be?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. This is an order issued by the commander of the Bratunac Brigade for an attack on Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, have you ever seen this document?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I personally received this document from the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, and I was duty-bound to sign for it and to read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, is there anywhere in this particular document that would be of particular interest for your unit?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: In this order for combat operations under item 6.1 and 6.2 -- just a moment, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If you could just -- I want to focus on that -- on those paragraphs now. Now, could you please explain to us what does paragraph 6 refer to.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 6, this refers to fire support of the brigade artillery for the defence of the town of Bratunac, according to the order issued by the commander of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, 6.1, I want to go down the list. Could you please explain to us what does that mean.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: 6.1 means that if any enemy movement is observed in these areas, where it says the Potocari school, they're not referring to the school building but to the area around the school, Pecista, that's a village in front of the front end of the Bratunac Brigade. Budak, Pale, and Cizmici also. All these are places on the line of the enemy defence in front of the front end of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Gavric, I want to go step by step. You see the paragraph that says 6.1 and then 6.11, 6.2. So I want to do it step by step. So just looking at 6.1, it says here: "The brigade consisting of 105-millimetre Howitzer platoon," is that you?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... millimetre gun platoon, is that also your unit?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And a B1 gun battery. Where were they located?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: The units of the brigade artillery were located behind the front end of defence of the Bratunac Brigade, behind the first line of defence, that is. And each of these batteries had its own area of operations and covered a certain area of defence of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What's in front of these platoons? What is the direction that they're facing?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Each artillery piece has to be set up on its firing position, when the firing position is taken up. The basic task of the commander of that firing position is to see what the direction is towards the enemy and the basic direction of an artillery piece can be 4 or 5 degrees to the right. I'm talking about how far it is from the main direction and the same to the left. Depending on the artillery piece itself, its range, it has to be established how far it is to be located from the first line of defence, which means in principle that if the units are on the defensive, then the artillery pieces have to be behind the front line for two-thirds of their range. For example, if the range of an artillery piece is 9.000 metres, the artillery piece has to be placed 6.000 metres behind the first line of defence, where its own units are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, we have four battalions in the Bratunac Brigade. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could just tell us in which battalion was this located, your position? The 1st, the 2nd, the 3rd, or the 4th?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: In the composition of the combat operations, the commanders of the batteries and the artillery monitors have to have their observation posts, if possible, at the first line or near the first line. And from this point, as far as is possible, they can have a good view of their own units and of the enemy positions. In this case, I'm talking about my particular case, my observation post was located on 438, or rather, on elevation 438, the Kalinsko Brdo. And this was part of the defence of the 2nd Infantry Battalion of the 1st Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So if we went to the map, we would be able to locate where your unit was?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. If we go to 6.11, your tasks. Just look at that document, and again we're referring to P406. I want to go one by one. 6.11. Now, I'm going to read it and then we're going to go through it. The first part, the subparagraph says: "Open fire on observed targets in the sector of the Potocari school, Peciste, Budak, Pale and Cizmici." Now, did this happen? Did you carry out this task?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: When an order for combat operations is drawn up, the platoon leaders are duty-bound to send the commander a suggestion concerning their units as to how and what they should do. The brigade commander studies all this and then reaches a decision on the use of these units and their tasks. In my proposal to the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, when drawing up the combat order, I proposed that artillery preparation should be carried out toward the enemy first line of defence, and thus simulate an effect from the direction of Bratunac in order to get the enemy to focus their forces on us. Because our task was to defend the town of Bratunac. The 1st Infantry Battalion, the 2nd Infantry Battalion, and the brigade artillery, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, getting back to my question, it says here: "Open fire on these observed targets." Did that occur?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let me go down to the next one. It says: "Prevent the enemy from introducing fresh forces from the depth toward their positions." To the best of your recollection, did you do anything to accomplish this task, to prevent the enemy from producing fresh forces from their depth toward their positions?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. The next task says: "Open barrage fire in the Potocari sector in case of possible attack, and prevent withdrawal of UNPROFOR weapons toward the depth of the enclave." Was this task carried out?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Barrage fire, yes, but prevent withdrawal of UNPROFOR weapons, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we're going to talk about the barrage fire, but I want to go first down the line so we'll come back to that. The next says: "Combat readiness at 0300 hours on 6 July 1995." Was this task accomplished? Were you ready by the period of time?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me go down to 6.2 and then we'll return to the barrage fire. 6.2, it says here that: "The 128-millimetre launcher platoon will provide support from the fire positions in the Kaolin sector." And then it says: "At 0300 hours on 6 July 1995, it will fire four projectiles, 50-kilogramme air bombs, on the Potocari sector." And then it says: "The school, the 11th of March factory, the Gracic hill, the coordinates, trig coordinates 377 Kula and Orici." Now, was this accomplished?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No. In this combat order, some corrections should be entered. I assume these are typing errors. The 128-millimetre launcher platoon was something we did not have. We had a 70-millimetre launcher, and this was handmade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But further down we -- okay. If we make that correction, aside from that, looking at this task, was it carried out, where it says: "0300 hours on July 6th." That's what I'm focusing your attention on.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: The readiness of the unit, yes, that did happen, but not the firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So what you're saying, if I understand you correctly, at 0300 hours on 6 July, you did not fire the four projectiles on the Potocari sector, as it states here in the order. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, let's go back to where you said that there was some barrage fire. Now, from this particular document, it would appear, it would appear, that the Srebrenica campaign began sometime in the early morning hours of July 6th. Is that your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we said that July 11th is the date when Srebrenica fell. So did you order your unit to commence any firing on the 6th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about the 7th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about the 8th?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about the 9th?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about the 10th, the day before Srebrenica fell?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about the 11th?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, could you please tell us where it was that this barrage fire took place, where did you order it and why?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: On the 11th, the 12th, 1995, at around 1400 hours, I observed a large-scale movement of the population from the direction of Srebrenica toward Bratunac. More precisely, from my observation post, I was able to see the entry into Srebrenica. I'm speaking of the road leading from Bratunac to Srebrenica. The Vidikovac neighbourhood, the Solocusac village, Kapetanova Cuprija, also known as Poligon. The local commune of Donji Potocari, and all the villages in front of the first line, that is in the Potocari area. While observing from the artillery observation post through the artillery equipment, the S61, I observed that in that mass of people there were many men in camouflage uniforms who were carrying weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you here. You said the observation post equipment, and then you said it was the S61. Could you please describe to us what equipment are you referring to.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: That is equipment for artillery observation. When a soldier who is in charge of observing adjusts the instrument and looks through it in the desired direction, it brings the desired target ten times closer so that at any point you can see it completely clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. From your position to where you saw the mass of people with the soldiers, as you described it, could you please tell us: What was the distance? What was their distance?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: As the crow flies, about 1.000 metres, which in practice seen through the document [as interpreted] is 100 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So could you please tell us what you were able to see with your equipment on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: On that day, that is the 11th, 12th of December, perhaps 1995, at around 1400 hours I observed long lines of men, women, children who were moving in the direction of the town of Bratunac. As I was in a very difficult situation, I had to respect the combat order, which says: "Open barrage fire to prevent enemy advances." In this case when I saw what kind of people were in that mass, I decided to correct this barrage fire at the expense of my own forces, to the detriment of my own forces, which means that I went 500 metres from our own front line and 3 kilometres away from the population who was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I want to clarify a couple of points. First of all, you indicated it was the 11th or 12th of December, 1995. We're talking about July -- 11 July 1995. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I -- yes, I mixed up months and dates. What I wanted to say was the 11th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, you said something about making a correction. Could you please tell us what did you mean when you said you decided to correct the barrage fire at the expense of your own forces? First of all, what is a correction?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Correction or adjustment is something that must be done if possible before using artillery to fire on a certain target, because of differences in time and temperature. At different temperatures, the range of artillery pieces changes. In this case, it was necessary to carry out the correction or adjustment. And you have to check on artillery hit on an imagined target in a certain area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. So is that sort of like a test firing when you say "making a correction"?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you were making this -- first of all, let me ask you this: Why did you think it was necessary to make this correction? You told us that you have to if you're going to use the equipment, but why did you think it was necessary to make the correction, because the assumption would be that at some point you're going to be using this equipment, this artillery, against someone or some target?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I have to say that correction or adjustment in this case viewed from my point of view had two positive effects. It -- one, it allowed your own forces on the defence line to know that if an attack would take place, they would be reinforced and have -- receive backup by us. And secondly, I am telling the enemy forces that they won't be able to pass through if they want to storm an entry into town. And at the same time, I was issuing a warning to the enemy side not to involve civilians who might be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, when you say "the enemy side who might involve civilians," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I am directly referring to the soldiers, not the civilians, because these soldiers are persons under arms, bearing arms, and who were in the 288th -- I'm sorry, 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, how did you know they weren't the DutchBat, the Dutch soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I was very well able to recognise the blue helmet soldiers, or rather, people from the DutchBat, the Dutch soldiers. Because they moved around in their vehicles going in front of the civilians. And at one point when I was angry, I was angry when I saw on these vehicles, on the driver's and co-driver's side and at the back of the vehicle, there were enemy soldiers in uniforms latching on. And I thought, and this was probably true, that certain people who had got their hands dirty wanted to find refuge in the base of the DutchBat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you ever see -- well, first of all, what was the number, if you can give us an approximation. You saw this mass of people and you see these soldiers that you identify as the 28th Division. Can you give us an estimation of how many there were that would cause you alarm to carry out this correction?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: In the entire group, that is to say the population who moved out of Srebrenica, including the women, the children, the elderly, and the soldiers, in my free estimation, there might have been about 40.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, that's 40.000 of all the people?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I said overall, including the women, children, elderly persons, civilians, and soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. What happened to those soldiers? Were you where ever able to see where they ultimately went?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: At one point in time when this mass of people, if I can put it that way, stopped in the industrial zone of Potocari - and I'm saying the 11th of May factory, the zinc factory, the Feros factory, and, or rather, the automobile transport company of Srebrenica, this was an area where this entire group of people stopped, all the people that moved out of Srebrenica. After a certain period of time you could notice that certain groups, certain groups of soldiers, were leaving the area, that space, and moving in the direction of Gornji Potocari, in the direction of Jaglic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know whether there is a road that heads in that direction?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is a village road or a macadamised road leading to the village of Jaglic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, did you fire at that group of soldiers that you saw that came with the mass of people and then left, did you fire at them?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Could you please tell us exactly what you did, where you fired. When you made this correction, what were you aiming at?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Two corrections or adjustments were made. One correction was made with the aim of barrage fire, intended in the front line of our defence and warning the enemy that they won't be able to pass through if they wanted to enter the town forcefully. The second was with the artillery pieces. The 122-military guns, cannons. And we carried out a correction on the Serbian village located right above Potocari. The slopes of that village, and it's called Studenac, are north facing, whereas I was on the southern slopes, south-facing slopes of Kalin hill, to I was very well able to look at the imagined artillery hits or corrections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Why were you making a correction on a Serbian village?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: That Serbian village I think numbers about five houses. And those houses had been burnt down to the ground, so there was nothing there, no soldiers, no civilians, and it served me very well to prepare my equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, after making those corrections, could you please tell us whether you carried out any barrage fire. Before the correction with the 105-millimetre Howitzers was carried out and the barrage fire, we did not engage in barrage fire anymore, we didn't need to. But we did target enemy forces who held the decisive defence at elevation 789 which was called Divljakinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, before we get to that, could you please tell us how close were you firing to the mass of people?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: About 3 to 4 kilometres away from that mass of people. If you mean the population, the inhabitants that had rallied in Potocari. So 3 to 4 kilometres away from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, are you firing behind them, are you firing to the side of them? In which direction? If they're coming down the road towards the industrial centre there in Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: The population that had fled from Srebrenica was located in the industrial centre zone, and the Divljakinje elevation or feature was located to the north-east of them. And the projectile curve could not have endangered that population, those people, because it was viewed to the left. It was to the left of the population and me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, was that the correction that you were carrying out, or was that the second firing to Divljakinje?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: In the course of the 11th of July, twice, I used the Howitzer 105-millimetre twice. The first time was for corrective purposes of the imaginary line in the defence of the town. And the second time was two hours later when I had noticed enemy forces located around Divljakinje, setting up their defence there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Did you at any time aim your fire at civilians?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, before carrying out the corrections and firing two hours later, did you receive any particular orders from your commander? You told us that you -- your immediate superior commander was Colonel Blagojevic. Did you receive any particular orders to carry out those tasks?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No, none. No orders during the combat operations, except a written combat order, the one that I had received prior to the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So if I understand you correctly, you were basing this order as the grounds for carrying out those tasks?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, did you contact your commander to let him know that you were about to carry out these activities?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: For me, as the chief of artillery, I had had a written order, and a written order was sufficient authorisation, giving me competency to use the -- to use and resort to artillery fire when and where necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But initially, earlier, you told us that you had endangered in some way your own men, you know, the brigade soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you -- well, first of all, explain to us what you meant by that.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: When you're shooting or using artillery pieces across your own forces, there must be a safety zone, as it's called. If an artillery -- for an artillery projectile, the closest that is allowed to fall near your own forces. And this safety margin depends on the weapons and their calibres. It is different for different artillery pieces. Most often this safety margin ranges from 300 to 600 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And why did you think it was some sort of a -- well, were you within that safety margin when you fired the corrections, you made the corrections?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: When I made those corrections, as I've already stated, in my assessment I had -- I would rather say that I had brought our own force's safety into question rather than the civilians. And in any artillery targeting, there is always a law of probabilities, and that firing can jeopardise -- by firing, you can jeopardise your own forces. But in this particular case, everything turned out fine, the way in which I had imagined it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I erred on the side of the safety of my own forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in light of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have a break now. We'll resume at quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Gavric, during that period from the 6th to the 11th, did you at any point in time fire in the -- in the direction of Srebrenica, targeting Srebrenica, the town itself?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, aside from your artillery unit, do you know whether the VRS, the Drina Corps, and other units that were there or that were -- they had artillery equipment on the ground being used at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: The artillery pieces, artillery equipment, was something that all the operational units had, those that were engaged in the attack on Srebrenica for their own support, fire-power support.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were you by any chance in communication with those units so you would be aware of what their activities were?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please explain to us, just very briefly, what sort of communication means you had from your location, say with the -- your own commander?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: We had a radio device. It was the RUP-12 or a Motorola of the M1000 type.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And could you communicate with the commander, assuming that he was in, say, Pribicevac, could you communicate with him with your radio?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I could, but I did not communicate because I had no need to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I understand that there is a rocket platoon in the Bratunac Brigade. Are you -- were you aware of that or am I correct in stating that?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct. There was a rocket piece, a rocket weapon, which was more for psychological purposes than as a piece of equipment that could actually achieve any great targeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Do you know who was the commander of that rocket platoon? Do you recall?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Who --

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Milos Loncarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And were you in charge of that rocket platoon, in light of your position as the commander of artillery?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Did you by any chance during those days, the 6th, the 7th, the 8th, the 9th, the 10th, the 11th, the 12th, or the 13th, did you give the rocket platoon any instructions or orders I should say to fire their equipment?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Incidentally, where were they located, if you recall, during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I think they were near elevation 438, to the west of my observation post.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you tell us whether you were aware of whether they had changed their position, the ones that they held previously to, in light of the attack on Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly whether they changed it, but that -- that was a mobile weapon and you were able to change its position, quickly change positions in line with circumstances and requirements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And if I understand you correctly - and I just want to make sure that we all are clear on this - on those days from the 6th to the 11th, the position -- your position had not changed to what it had been previously. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Since the beginning of the war and the establishment of the Bratunac Brigade and the defence of the Bratunac Brigade, my observation post was always at elevation 438, Kalinsko hill, until the end of the operation at Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to go through some documents. But perhaps before I do that, let me ask you: Did you fire again at any targets, aside from the two that you told us, on the 12th, the 13th, the 14th, the 15th, the 16th, did you fire artillery equipment?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: After the 11th of July, the artillery did not have any need to fire at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, before we discuss what you did after this day, I want to go through some documents, the first one being Prosecution Exhibit 411. You'll have 411/B, which is the Srpski version. If you could look at that. What is this, sir, this document?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: This document is a combat report, which is -- which was sent out daily to the command of the Drina Corps, and it speaks about the activities of the brigade over a period of 24 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And -- well, what day is this daily report, combat daily report? If you look at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: As far as I can see in the lower right-hand corner, you can see this. But it's not legible at the top. It says the 6th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, if you go to paragraph number 2 and look at the second paragraph in that numbered paragraph, it states, does it not: "Firing support against set targets was provided by 70-millimetre shell launcher." And then in parenthesis, it says: "(School at Potocari, 11th March factory and wide area to the village of Potocari"). Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, earlier you told us that in spite of the order of 5 July 1995, paragraphs 6.2, that you had not carried out that particular task, and I'm referring to Prosecution Exhibit 406. Do you recall me asking you whether you had carried out the task listed in the commander's order of 5 July, paragraph 6.2?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Please, take a look at the combat report and paragraph 6 of it, I think, where it says how much artillery and infantry ammunition was spent. And it says that infantry ammunition, 7.62, 5.000 pieces; mortar shells, 120-millimetres, ten pieces; and mortar shells, 82-millimetres, 20 pieces. Which testifies to the fact that none of these weapons were within the composition of the brigade artillery, but it was the artillery group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I just want to make sure I follow your answer. By looking at paragraph 6 in this daily combat report, are you suggesting that it's somewhat contradictory of paragraph 2?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely what I'm saying. Somebody -- the person who wrote this report should have, in paragraph 2, stipulated the fact that fire-power support at certain targets was carried out by battalion fire groups and not the artillery brigade, because point 2 and point 6 of this combat report are contradictory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And so I take it just to make sure that in spite of looking at this daily combat report of 6 July 1995, you stand firm behind your previous testimony, that on that particular day you did not fire your weapons?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if I can go on to the next document, and this is Prosecution Exhibit 412. And this would be 412/B for you. Do you recognise -- well, what is this document?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: This is again a daily combat report to the command of the Drina Corps. I have it in handwriting, the printed part is not legible. And it's dated the 7th of July, 1995, if that's the one you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That is the one that I am referring to. Now, if you could please look at paragraph 2, sir. It says: "Our forces returned the fire and also fired artillery at the enemy's firing positions." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: This is paragraph 2 in the daily combat report. Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That is what I'm referring to. Do you see that? The first sentence of paragraph number 2.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: A large number of combat reports I understood were done mechanically, according to a pattern, without looking at the reports from the field. The person who was on duty that day and drew up this combat report mixed up the battalion firing group and the brigade artillery. And this is not one and the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So are you suggesting, sir, that this daily combat report dated 7 July 1995 that has been identified as Prosecution Exhibit 412, to your understanding, knowledge, and belief, it does not reflect what occurred with respect to your unit on that particular day?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: This document does not reflect the situation of my unit on the 7th of July. It cannot be the way it's stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Let me show you another document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ARGIBAY
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Karnavas. Could you please take a look at page 31, I think line 23. And I think the witness said when clarifying about the combat report on the battalion firing group and the brigade artillery. He said this is not one and the same thing and the transcript has omitted the "not." That changes the thing absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That's -- yes. Yes. I -- thank you very much, Judge Argibay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Going -- I'm trying to figure out how to rephrase it now. In your earlier answer, you indicated that whoever wrote this combat report mixed up their facts. Could you please again clarify for us -- would you please clarify for us how is it that you believe that the duty officer who wrote the daily combat report was mistaken with respect to paragraph 2 as it relates to artillery.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: To clarify, within the composition of the brigade, there is a brigade artillery. Whereas I said, there is 122-millimetre gun battery, 105-millimetre Howitzer, and B1 76-millimetre guns. Within the battalion, as battalion artillery support, there are platoons of 82-millimetre mortars, 120-millimetre mortars, and recoilless guns. Looking at this paragraph of the combat report of the 7th of July, I can see that the duty officer who drew up this report does not distinguish between the battalion firing group and the brigade artillery group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, if we could go on to the next document, and this is -- this has been introduced as -- or has an identification number of D131.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I apologise for this delay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, sir, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And I take it you have the handwritten version in Srpski. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, was this document ever shown to you by the Office of the Prosecution when you met with them and you gave an eight-hour statement as a witness back on 28 November, 2001?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, for interrupting. We actually don't have a copy of that document. I don't know if Mr. Karnavas has an extra copy for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, did you furnish this document to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Because it's a new document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: They furnished us with this document, so it's part of their disclosure material. But if we haven't, as part of our obligation prior to coming here, I apologise. But we should have an extra copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you recall whether this document was shown to you by the investigator in Banja Luka when you met with them on the 28th of November, 2001?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we could just look at the document first. All right. First of all, could you tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: This is a report on the consumption of materiel and equipment and ammunition in the period from the 10th of July to the 12th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please tell us who generated, who made this document? Do you see any signature lines that would give you some sort of an indicator as to who was responsible for creating this document?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: The signature is not completely legible, but in my view this would be the signature of Dragan Trisic, who was the assistant commander for logistics. He was a major by rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in looking at this particular document, could you please tell us, as we can see on the left side there are numbers 1 to 17, which of the numbers referring to materiel used, which of these numbers relate to your unit?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: As for my unit, the numbers that relate to it are numbers 14, 105-millimetre Howitzer; number 15, 122-millimetre, it says here Howitzer, but in fact it should be a gun M-31/30.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. What about number 13, the 100-millimetre T-55? Does that refer to your unit?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No. That is a tank, a self-propelled artillery piece, which did not belong to the brigade artillery group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So to your knowledge, this particular document has on number 14 and number 15 the -- at least it reflects the consumption of materiel that would have been used from the period of 10 July to 12 July, 1995. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, in looking at point 14, it says: "Bullets, 105-millimetre Howitzer," and then if we go all the way to the right it says: "60 pieces." To the best of your knowledge, would that figure be accurate?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: You should say 105-millimetres, not 100. As for 60 pieces, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, when would -- when were those consumed, if you know? The 10th? The 11th? Or the 12th?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: This was used on the 11th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And again, you indicated that there were two firing positions, there was the one correction, and then two hours later you had the firing towards Divljakinje. So which of the two are we talking about, if we look at number 14?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: The consumption of ammunition for the 105-millimetre Howitzer refers to the correction that was carried out, that is the preparation for the barrage fire, and the targeting of targets on Divljakinje, 7, 8, and 9. This was done by one unit, and it used this amount of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we go to number 15, where you indicated this is incorrectly stated, it has 20 pieces. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, again, could you please tell us first of all, does this figure of 20 pieces accurately reflect the amount of shells consumed during that period, the 10th, the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And could you please tell us how were they consumed or where were they consumed, in which direction?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: If you will allow me to clarify this, I can do so right away.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: When taking up firing positions with artillery pieces, the crews and commanders of the firing position are duty-bound to rectify or adjust the targeting equipment using an artillery -- using artillery equipment. In this case, the commander of the firing position made an error. And when designating the fundamental direction of the 122-millimetre, he did not carry out rectification of the equipment, the sights. When I ordered him to correct this equipment, the sights, toward the village of Studenac, which was above Potocari on the northern slopes of the hill, I noticed that rectification of the sights and the angle-measuring equipment and distance-measuring equipment had not been carried out, because from the hit of the projectile, I did not hit the envisaged target. At that time I was very angry. I called the commander of this firing position and ordered him to carry out, as soon as possible, rectification of the sights and the distance-measuring equipment, and he did this right away. When they had completed this, they reported to me to say that the artillery pieces were ready for the correction. Then we continued carrying out the correction in view of our intended target, and very soon we achieved the desired effect and hit the envisaged target, that is the village of Studenac. To clarify this a little bit, an artillery hit is not a hit on one point but on an area, because artillery pieces of different calibres cover wider areas. They have bigger hits.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, I began -- now, before coming here today, have you had a chance to look at your statement, the statement that you gave to the investigator over that eight-hour period back on 28 November 2001?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Until I arrived here, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now -- but before coming here, before testifying today, you were provided with a copy of your statement for you to read and look over?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I said I didn't have an opportunity of seeing it until I arrived in The Hague, but when I arrived in The Hague I was given this document and I read my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, in reading your statement did you notice the area in the statement where you were asked about this particular document?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, in your statement at that point in time, when you were questioned by Dean Manning, do you recall what your answer was, having been shown this document?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would you please tell us what your answer was when he confronted you with this document and asked you questions with respect to the consumption of materiel, as it related to your unit?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: As the gentleman, the investigator, showed me this document, I only noticed the 12th of July as the date here. And that's why I said the document was incorrect, because my units did not fire any ammunition on that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, that document, does it say the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: On the document it says the period from the 10th to the 12th of July, 1995. But at the time, I didn't notice this, I didn't notice that it said 10 to 12th. I only noticed the 12th of July as the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, at the beginning -- at the top of this document, what does this say as far as date is concerned?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. If you look at the very top of the page, it says -- it tells us what date it is, does it not? The very top on the left side. Do you see where it says St. Peter's Day, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I don't see a date, but I see a description of the day. It says: "St. Peter's Day, 1995."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I apologise for phrasing my question inartfully. Tell us, do you know what day that is, St. Peter's Day?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: St. Peter's Day is on the 12th of July. On that day, my unit did not fire. This is the report delivered by the assistant commander for the consumption of materiel and equipment, for the period from the 10th to the 12th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, could you please tell us -- well, you told us that from the -- from that point onwards, you did not use your artillery equipment again. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would you tell us, if you recall, when you received your next order.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Could you please tell us when it was, the date.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: That was on the 14th or the 15th of July, or to be more precise at 00 hours or at 0020 hours in the command of the Bratunac Brigade, from the brigade commander, Colonel Vidoje Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Could you please describe to us or tell us what was the order that you received between, you know, the 14th and the 15th of July.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: The order was about the use of my unit, the Zvornik Brigade, to secure the Zvornik/Sekovici/Tuzla communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Could you be a little more concrete. What exactly was being asked of you by your commander?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: He asked that I order and lead my unit and take it to Zvornik to report to the command of the Zvornik Brigade. And from there I would be deployed to secure the above-mentioned communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Were you being asked to also take the artillery equipment with you?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, no. At that point in time, my unit had orders to be used as an infantry unit. And I did not like this at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, could you tell us what happened.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: When the commander told me, or rather, gave me this order, for the first time in my military career I refused an order. I was angry and so was my commander. We were angry at each other. I asked that I be issued a written order. I wanted to have a written document ordering me to take my unit along an unsafe road with only infantry weapons and go to carry out a task on unknown terrain where I was not familiar with anything. Because there was a large chance that we might be killed even before we reached the place where we were supposed to carry out this task. To explain this further, in those days the enemy forces were breaking through from the direction of Srebrenica towards Tuzla. And in several places, there was a danger of all of us getting killed because the communication of the road cut through terrain across which they were moving. That was one thing. Another thing was that we were going together with the units that had quite different training and was not as well prepared and as well armed. And I felt they could not oppose in infantry fighting an enemy that was superior in numbers and weapons. I did not want to go and carry out this task where something ugly might have happened. I might have survived, but a lot of men -- that's why I wanted a written document. I wanted it to be known who ordered this; however, I was not given a written document. After a certain time, I did accept, I did agree to go, because the commander promised that he would relieve me on the following day. During this conversation when I was receiving this order, Dragan Trisic was present. He left the room at one point. He was probably surprised by my reaction. When the commander officially told me that these orders had come from higher up, I understood that it was not up to him and that I was putting him in an unpleasant situation. So we set out and at 0100 hours, we set off towards Zvornik. On the way -- well, we arrived safely in the command of the Zvornik Brigade --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a second. About what time did you leave the Bratunac Brigade and head towards the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was about 0100 hours on the 15th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How many men were with you?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: About 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How long did it take you to get to the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: 40 to 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived there, do you -- had you been to the Zvornik Brigade command before?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, when you went there, could you please tell us what you did.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I arrived at the command of the Zvornik Brigade, I went to find the duty officer because as it was around 0200 hours there was just the assistant deputy officer there. So I reported to him and said that I had arrived from Bratunac, and that I had orders to report there. That person - I don't remember whether he was an officer or an NCO, or whatever - he told me that the officer or rather Obrenovic was sleeping because he was tired. And I asked him to convey to him that we had arrived and that we should be deployed and given our assignment. He went out, he left and when he returned he told us that we were told to stay within the factory compound, in the premises there, and that we would stay there until further notice, and if necessary we would be informed. And that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, when he said that Obrenovic was sleeping, did you know who he was referring to?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Probably or quite certainly he was thinking of the chief of staff of the Zvornik Brigade, that Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, on page 42, line 22 or 21, there was just an assistant deputy officer there. Deputy or the duty officer? It's important.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, we're going to -- thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, who was -- when you got there, who did you report to?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I reported first of all to the reception area where there was a military policeman providing security to the entrance to the brigade headquarters. Then after that, he showed me where the operations room of the Zvornik Brigade was located. And it was in this room that I came upon the deputy duty officer, because from 0000 hours to the morning hours, the regulation was that the deputy duty officer was on duty, whereas the duty officer would be on duty until 00 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And it was this officer that made a reference to Obrenovic, the deputy duty officer?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: The deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. At that point in time, did you know Major Jokic?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I don't remember ever having met the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now -- so you were told to stay there. Where did you stay overnight?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: We stayed in a room -- or actually, it was a factory. The soldiers were put up there, and I spent most of the time outside. Because it was summertime and dawn broke early. So we stayed to the end, or rather, to the shift. We didn't leave the command area of the Zvornik Brigade, and we weren't deployed anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, the next morning, did you by any chance see Mr. Obrenovic there -- then to get your next orders now that you had reported to the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't see him or report to him. They knew I had arrived and that I was ready and waiting. And if necessary, I thought that he would let me know and inform me what was needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, did anyone from the Zvornik Brigade, be it Obrenovic or the duty officer of the day, did they ever contact you? And we're speaking now of July 15th, 1995, the morning hours.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Nobody. After my arrival and my reporting contacted me at all, until the arrival of Major Eskic from the Bratunac Brigade who took one of the companies from the 2nd Infantry Battalion led by the commanding officer of the Company, Zoran Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I want to break this down and I want to go step by step. First of all, who is Major Eskic?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Major Eskic, his first name was Dragan, his second name was Eskic, was a personnel officer in the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And at what time did Major Eskic arrive -- what time did you see him?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, that was between 10.00 and 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And how did he arrive?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: They arrived by bus. He got off the bus. He was the first to get off the bus, and behind him was the commanding officer of the company, Zoran Kovacevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you know Zoran Kovacevic at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Did you have a conversation with Major Eskic?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I talked to Major Eskic, and he told me that the commander, Blagojevic, had ordered them to come and replace me, relieve me, as we had agreed, I and my commander. So that the commander sent Major Eskic on behalf of the brigade command, and that was standard practice. He did that fairly frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would you please tell us at what time you returned or you left for the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I know that it was about 12.00, or rather, I was in Bratunac at about 12.00. And it was soon after Major Eskic arrived that I ordered the lining up of unit. We took the bus, and I took that same bus back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, before Major Eskic's arrival, before he came, on that particular morning, 15 July 1995, did you encounter any other individuals there, any officers?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: At around 8.30 or 9.00, when I arrived at the entrance gate and the reception area, I met a young man, nicely dressed in an all-in-one suit. And as far as I knew him, I think he was Lukic. And he tried to talk to me. I was to give him some of my men to go with him on one of his assignments. I refused to do that. And there was a very unfortunate exchange, but I don't know what the other man was by rank. He was the security man Drago Nikolic. He involved himself in our heated conversation, and the late Dusko Nikolic, he's deceased today, he was also a school friend of mine. He was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
