utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you this: You mention Lukic. Does he have a first name?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I don't know his first name. I don't know it to this day after all this time. All I know is they referred to him as Lukic. I heard a lot of ugly things about him, bad things about him. And he wasn't at my level. He was a soldier, or whatever. But he wasn't in a position to issue any orders to me, let alone me give him my men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Do you know where Mr. Lukic was from? Did you know at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: At that time, I did not know. Today, I do know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And where is he from, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was from the surrounding parts of Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, once you -- incidentally, when you returned to the Bratunac Brigade, did you inform your commander of Mr. Lukic's request, that is for you to give him some men for whatever assignment he was carrying out at the time?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I don't think I did, because I didn't think I needed to do that, so I didn't. I didn't give my men to anybody without having received previous authorisation and instructions to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So you returned, I take it, if you left around noon, by 1.00 or so on the 15th of July, 1995, you should have been back in Bratunac. Could you please tell us what you did for the rest of that day.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Upon returning from that assignment, I went back to the command of the Bratunac Brigade. I let the unit go and have a rest, because there were no other assignments or tasks. I returned. I came upon my commander there. And I said hello to him. We were on friendly terms, and we were satisfied that we had respected our -- each other's orders, or rather, I respected his order and the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, on the 16th, were you given any assignments? 16th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. What about the 17th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what assignment you received on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: From the afternoon of the 15th to the 17th in the morning, I had days off, free days. My commander gave me that free time off. And on the 17th, the 17th was a Monday, the 17th of July was a Monday to the best of my recollections, I received orders, an oral order to take part of my unit of the 3rd Infantry Battalion that he led. I think he was Lieutenant Colonel Zekic. His name was Dragan Zekic, I believe. And part of the Workers' Battalion. Actually, he was a 2nd Lieutenant. So I was told to go to the area of Kravica, or more exactly to the Sandici bend by Krajinovici village and Kamenica village and to reconnoiter the terrain there for certain groups and search the area to see that there weren't any stragglers in the Konjevic Polje area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Where were you when you received this order?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I received that order in the headquarters, in our hall there, where we would usually be given orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Aside from Dragan Zekic of the 3rd Infantry Battalion, was there anyone else assigned or with you to carry out this task of searching the terrain?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I don't know about the other units, except for part of the 3rd Battalion and the Workers' Battalion. So I did not know about the others until I reached the terrain, whether any other unit would be joining us in searching the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. When you got to the terrain, incidentally, were you given coordinates as to where -- what section of the terrain, on the map? Were you given coordinates where you should carry out this searching operation?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't need to. I was born in the area, so I knew it very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, when you got to the terrain, were there any other units in the terrain that were also there to conduct or to assist in this searching operation?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you please tell us which units were there.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Apart from our own units from Bratunac, from the Bratunac Brigade, the ones that I mentioned, I found there another unit, a unit of the special police, commanded by Dusko Jevic, nicknamed Staljin. They say that they were the special forces, but I say that they were Serb deserters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: In that unit comprised of all the men who were brought in through certain channels from Serbia, and my sister's son was among the men there. So they had deserted, they had fled, and they were engaged in other business. And I don't know through which channels they happened to be in the special police, but that's what they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, could you please tell us when you got to the terrain and you found this MUP unit what you, Mr. Zekic, and Dusko Jevic, also known as Staljin, did.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: At that point in time when the unit was lined up, at that bend, when I say unit, I mean the unit of the Bratunac Brigade, I told Zekic that we would be searching the terrain in a column, in line. And Dusko said we should divide up the terrain, that he would take his units to search the terrain from the communication line, the road, from the asphalt road and go as far as he was able to. When he deployed these -- when these units were deployed, I remember that the special detachment of that police arrived below the village of Kamenica, somewhere in that area. So we travelled together, we went in column together. The soldiers were behind us, and we would deploy each soldier and told him which direction to take in our search. So Dule issued orders to his men and I issued orders to my men. In moving around the terrain, there's a village path, a road, a village road. So looking at it from Kravica and Konjevic Polje and Bratunac to Sandic hill, to the left, toward those villages, or rather that line that we were supposed to take up and have as our departing point, point of departure in searching the terrain. And what I can tell you is this: It was a terrible sight to behold. Although I had already had four years of wartime experience, but what I came across was an enormous number of enemy soldiers who were dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Let me stop you here for a second. We're going to talk about that. First, you need to slow down a little bit so everything is being translated. Polako, polako.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I just needed to cover some points before we get to what you saw. You talked about Dusko Jevic being there, the commander of the MUP. But we also now have you, a commander; as well as Mr. Zekic, who is also a commander. Who is in charge?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: If you recall, what I said a moment ago was that the commander, Colonel Blagojevic, would often and usually when he thought that precise information should arrive from the terrain and that everything should be done properly, as he had envisaged it, he would always send out somebody -- one of us from the command, from the brigade command. This particular time I was sent on that assignment, I was given that task. And because everybody would receive written or oral orders, and my commander's orders were as follows, these were his final words: If you take enemy soldiers prisoner or civilians prisoner, you should act pursuant to the convention governing prisoners of war. And you can check this out in all the written orders issued by my commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. When you got to the terrain, was Mr. Zekic along with you, with his men?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Zekic was with me almost the whole time, right up until the end of that particular operation. And as Zekic at that moment was feeling a little ill, he had back pains, so he found it difficult to move around that kind of terrain. And we decided once we had deployed the units and issued them their assignments, Zekic had personal links with his superiors that we could go down the communication road from which we would be able to observe what was going on in the terrain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What about Dusko Jevic? Did he proceed along with his men, or was he hanging back with you and Mr. Zekic?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Dusko Jevic also issued orders of the kind we did. And together with Zekic, he went along the communication road towards Konjevic Polje, and his units were in physical contact with our units. His left flank and our right frank viewed from the Bratunac direction towards Konjevic Polje, on the left side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We have a couple of minutes left before it's time for a break, but if you could tell us very briefly: What is it that you saw, that site that you talked about, when you got to that part of the terrain as you were searching it on the morning of the 17th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: When we got to the departure point, I first of all came across a path which might have been 4 or 5 metres wide, and I gained the impression that a whole herd of animals had passed that way. I couldn't have imagined that men would have left a trace like that. There was just one or two sharp stones sticking out, but anyway which would have led me to deduce that a large group of people might have actually passed by that way, which I found out later on. When I reached this vantage point, I found many people who had hung themselves with their belts. I saw many people who had committed suicide by shooting themselves under the chin and the bullet passing through their bodies. I saw many people who had placed a bomb under themselves. I saw many people with irregular type wounds that were probably caused by artillery shots that hit them. And when I say "artillery," I know that along that axis there was the special police detachment equipped with Praga weapons, and I assume that some of them were wounded with those weapons. There were large groups on a whole open space, for example, people who were dead, who had been killed. And I learned about that when I handed over certain people during that assignment. I learnt that some shock bombs or mines were used that I had never encountered before, dumb grenades as they're called. And sometimes somebody would do so much shooting until he was shot himself by somebody in that mass of people. Now, I take up a little bit of time here but I have to tell you a an anecdote, something that I experienced. When I was training, doing my internship in Pozarevac, I was in the 3rd Garrison regiment, and General Petar Gracanin had decorated not only me, as being a good soldier and officer, commanding officer, but there was a luncheon and we asked him how he came to be limping. And he said he had this limp from the battle of Sutjeska during World War II, and he told us the story of how you could go for hours and days at Sutjeska encountering one body after another, jumping across bodies. And at the same time, I backtracked and remembered what had happened some 20 years previously when I, going from the village of Kamenica down to Konjevic Polje, that I could have passed that route without stepping on the ground. I stepped on one body after another. So anybody who had been there would know just how many corpses there were. It was an absolutely dreadful, horrific sight to have witnessed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I think it's time for a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Ms. Issa just went into this -- the room here outside. She should be here any second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll wait for a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Gavric, when we left off, we were on 17 July 1995, when you were searching the terrain. Now, could you please tell us what happened during that searching operation.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: During the searching operation, in the afternoon hours Zekic told me that our units had come across some minor resistance. I said to him that our units should be stopped, as our units and enemy units were in close proximity. I said to Zekic that they should call upon the enemy units to surrender, say that there were a large number of us, and that we should try to avoid loss of life. If they did not listen to us, we could introduce technical equipment. At that point, I received a report that a child between the ages of 9 and 11 had set out towards our units holding a white tee-shirt in their hand and waving it up high. I said to them that they should send the child back and that the child should say to those people that they should surrender to avoid any other problems. The child at first didn't want to do that, but at the insistence of our soldiers probably, it did go back. And shortly afterwards, there was a fight among their units. As far as we were able to ascertain later on, some of them were in favour of surrendering and others were not. At that point, the child came back followed by a certain number of men. I said to them that they should take certain positions and that those who wanted to surrender should lay down their weapons, raise their hands, and put their hands behind their necks, which is what they did. This was at the village of Pobudze, the hamlet of Rahunici, where there used to be a four-year elementary school. This was quite close to the road, and we ordered them to bring them to us. When they did that, I ordered that they be lined up, that they should lie down, put their hands on their backs, and that their hands should be tied. In the vicinity, there was a meadow, and there was some raspberries near that meadow. Raspberry plants are fragile and they have to be tied up with twine. So the twine was taken from those raspberry bushes, and these peoples' hands were tied. When these people were lined up, I noticed that in the group there were also minors. I asked that someone who had documents showing that they had been born after 1980 should present these; however, they had no documents. But I based my judgement on their appearance and I judged that there were three children among them. I immediately withdrew the children from the line-up. They were not tied up. And I ordered the soldiers that no one was to be maltreated or interfered with in any way. There was an unusual situation with regard to the children. There was a soldier who they addressed as a volunteer, and he wanted to liquidate those children. I ordered the soldiers to take that man away and disarm him. They said: "Why are you doing this since they're killing our children?" I said to them: "You're probably not a soldier and not a Serb." According to the ethics of a Serbian soldier, one never kills someone who is elderly, infirm, imprisoned, because they are all protected, especially those who surrender. They probably have good intentions, and that is why they must have protected status. The children went out on to the asphalt road where my driver was. Milan Nedeljkovic was his name. Soon after that, I spoke to Momir Nikolic and I told him that he should send buses for our men and that I had a certain number of men who had surrendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there for a second. Where was Momir Nikolic when you spoke to him?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Momir Nikolic - this was in the afternoon - was in the operations room.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, getting back to that incident, I'm not sure whether I understood you correctly. When you were talking about the one soldier who wanted to liquidate the children, was it he who said or they being the soldiers that you told to take this man away that protested and said: Why not, since they've done it to our children?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I will clarify. He wanted to take those children and probably liquidate them. He asked me why I was protecting them. He wanted to tell me that Muslim soldiers had killed our Serbian children in this way. I ordered one of the soldiers from that group, from the 3rd Battalion, to take that man away. And then I asked him whether he was a soldier and a Serb. He told me that he was a volunteer. I had never seen him before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, when you called Momir Nikolic and you asked for the buses, what was his response, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, he said that the buses would come, that the prisoners were to be sent to Konjevic Polje with Dusko Jevic, he probably knew about this. He said that Dusko was with us. And he said that somebody from Konjevic Polje would take them over, probably to take them to the camp that existed in the area of Bijeljina. This is what I did. Dusko Jevic took over the men. He lined them up two-by-two. He secured them with his men, and right away he set out in the direction of Konjevic Polje, because we were near Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That was my next question. How close were you to Konjevic Polje at this particular point in time?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: A kilometre or maybe a kilometre and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, why didn't you send them towards Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I didn't send them in the direction of Bratunac for the following reason: 30 or more men had to be taken to Bratunac by bus for 20 kilometres, then the buses would have to go back to go to Bijeljina. It was more logical because there was a collection centre, there was security for these men from Konjevic Polje to be taken to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Did you ever hear about what happened to these men that you handed over to Dusko Jevic?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, no. But the other day -- the following day I was going about my private business - and I said this in my statement of the 27th of November, 1992 -- 2002 - I saw them in a warehouse and I thought they were all there. But a policeman from the special police did not let me go there, and while I was talking to him, somebody probably recognised me. And from that point on, I lost track of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. What about the children? What happened to the children?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: That's a special story. For all normal people, the story is so difficult at times but also interesting at times. First, they lied to me. They said that two of those boys who are well-dressed and looked very nice, they were quite pretty, they said they were from Karacici, that their parents had walked into a minefield and been killed, and that they had gone with that group of people. I asked the third boy where he was from. He said that he was from Kasaba, that his father had been killed or was missing and he was going with this group. I asked them: "Well, then why did you surrender? Do you know who I am?" And they said: "Yes, we do." And I said to them: "I am a Chetnik officer." And they laughed and they said: "You're no Chetnik. A Chetnik has blood up to his elbows, a Chetnik has a long beard and an insignia of crossed knives, and you are dressed very nicely." I laughed at them and I patted them on the head and I said to Milan that they should be given something to eat. I had asked what they'd had to eat in the last few days, and they said they had eaten snails and that somebody had shot a boar and that they had found berries in the woods. They started playing in the asphalt road and one of them said: "It's so nice here where there were no mines around," because these children had been under great stress. Then they got in the car with me, the official vehicle. We joked and chatted along the way. And when I arrived in the command of the Bratunac Brigade, I took the children to the military police, where I found some policemen eating some meat. And I said that the children should be given clothes, that they should be allowed to wash, that they should be given something to eat. And I wanted to see the room where the children would sleep. And I said that the children should be given medical attention, so that everyone would know they had not been killed. When I left them there, they weren't happy. They wanted to stay with me. Probably they saw me as someone who provided safety for them. However, I went home. My home was some 200 metres away from the command of the Bratunac Brigade. And in the morning, I'm now speaking of the 18th of July, I found those children. They were cheerful. I asked them how they were. I asked if they were hungry. They were all satisfied and happy. After that, I received information that Miso Pelemis had been looking for me. I didn't know Miso Pelemis, but on one occasion we had met in passing briefly. He asked me whether I would allow him to exchange those children for certain of his men who had been taken prisoner in the area of Zvornik. I think this was a group of policemen from Doboj, as far as I knew, eight policemen and one komandir. I said yes, on one condition that the children be taken for exchange. Soon after that he arrived in a white open jeep. The children were not happy with my decision. I explained to them that I had business of my own to attend to, and that this gentleman would take them away to give them back to their families. When they set out, they waved to me, but they were a little bit confused. This was a difficult moment for me. I knew that these children were now leaving, but I was happy that I had, as I thought, done something humane. And I think that those children soon found their parents -- in fact, I know that for a fact now. Some of them are almost married. I heard this from Mr. Naser Oric, also known as Gazda, because in 2003, or rather, 2002 on the 1st of September, I attended a lunch in the Tuzla Hotel in Tuzla, and he told me that one of these young men had got married and that they had lied to me because those two pretty boys were the sons of his uncle, his first cousin. Knowing that their last name was Oric, they thought if they told me their real names, they would probably be liquidated. But whatever their last names, this would not have happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, earlier on you said that you wanted them to have medical attention. Was it medical attention or some sort of other attention so that everybody would know that those children were okay?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. Let me clarify. I asked that those children have a change of clothes, that they be given a bath. And we had doctors in the town who could examine them, because those children had travelled for days. If they set out on the 12th, and it was already the 17th, they had been in bad conditions, bad for an adult, let alone a child. I wanted them to have a medical checkup so that there would be a record that those children had been in Bratunac and there was nothing wrong with them. And I think that this document has to be still in existence with the Serbian television.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now, aside from this -- well, while we're still at it. You said that -- we talked about you giving a statement to the Prosecution on the 28th of November, 2001. You indicated today that when you got to the terrain, you learned that there was Dusko Jevic there with his MUP unit, and you also told us about Mr. Zekic. Now, in your statement to the Prosecution -- and I can give you a copy of it. I just want to make a reference to a couple of lines and give you an opportunity to comment on it. And this is on page 29, line 5. You were asked a question by Mr. Manning: "Okay. Were you in command of this group of men?" And your answer was: "I was not in command of that group, if you understood, but I came on behalf of the command of the brigade just to link them up -- link up the police and Zekic because they didn't know each other personally." Could you please explain to us what you meant by that when you gave your statement to the investigator from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: In this statement, which I made in Banja Luka, I was a commanding officer in the Bratunac Brigade who had been given orders to go and be with the subordinate units on the ground in order to have this job completed in a normal way and for our commander to know about this in full. I was directly responsible at that time for the units of the Bratunac Brigade. Dusko Jevic was a partner, not a subordinate. My responsibility and his responsibility were equal. He was answerable for his units, and I was answerable for what the Bratunac units -- the units of the Bratunac Brigade were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, this is the 17th of July. By this point in time, had you heard whether there had been any atrocities?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I did hear that there had been atrocities in the area of Kravica, but I didn't know any details about this. It was not part of my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But I take it you knew of the Kravica incident before this particular day when you were searching the terrain?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't think I knew about it before, because this was a very broad area. At the time I had my own duties, I didn't know where the 1st Infantry Company, the 1st platoon was going. I heard about this from colleagues, from friends, who talked about it later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. When you handed the prisoners on the 17th of July to Dusko Jevic, as Momir Nikolic had instructed you to do, what did you expect or what were you expecting to happen to those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Every normal person - when I say "normal person," I'm referring to the officers who were in that operation - and in my view the order which I had heard issued orally was that there would be a camp in the area of Bijeljina and that all those who surrendered would be taken to that camp to be exchanged for Serbs from the Tuzla basin and the Sarajevo basin. So I expected that those prisoners would be taken there and then exchanged.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I take it since then, since that period of time, you must have learned about what happened to a lot of the Muslim prisoners that were either captured or turned themselves over or were separated at Potocari?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: You mean in that period or do you mean until today?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I'm saying by today you must have heard what had happened -- what has happened.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: The whole world has heard about those events, and so have I. But I don't have any information about this. I only know there was killing. I know that there was certain groups who did this, that this was not done by organised units. That's as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to show you a document. I'm going to switch over to another period of time. I want to show you a document that has been marked as P98. It's been marked for identification purposes. Please look at it first. Now, in the translation it says: "Report to the brigade members." And then it says: "Submitted," and it would be to the unit of the 3rd Infantry Battalion. And the Srpski version, does it state: "Report"?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What does it state there?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: It says: "Information."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, is there a difference between information and a report?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: In all cases, as in this one, there does exist a difference. An information like this, the assistant commander for morale guidance and religious affairs would write this kind of information; whereas, a report is compiled by a commander officer for a specific unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Is there a difference between information and an order?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Similarly, every order must be addressed or must refer to a prior order. So either going from top to bottom or bottom to top; whereas, this doesn't exist here. It must be terms of reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, the date here is 4 July 1994. And the last page we have the name of Lieutenant Colonel Slavko Ognjenovic. Did you know this individual?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And who was he, sir? Who was he?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Slavko Ognjenovic I think was for two and a half years the commander of the Bratunac Brigade. And an officer that I would not like to encounter frequently, because his goals were to be a colonel or a general. He didn't think of the price, at all costs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And this information here, had you seen this -- back in 1994, had this been distributed to you to look at and to perhaps even implement?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember, I did not receive this and I wasn't that interested, because this piece of information, the one that I'm looking at now and have before we here, my commander wanted through that piece of information to demonstrate to somebody just how great a commander he was. And that he can see further than others. So I considered that through this piece of information he just wished to aggrandise himself and put himself above others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, if we could just look at the first paragraph, first number of paragraphs. Reading it, if you could read it to yourself, and tell us what do you derive from this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: This is a purely information given out by the commander, lieutenant colonel, I assume he wrote this. And he is putting forth an idea that somebody from the Main Staff would arrive and that the units should be placed on combat readiness, and that they should be at the ready to demonstrate this situation which was good, fairly good. That's how I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now -- and who was the commander that -- this is Ognjenovic that we're talking about. Right?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This is the information he signed, as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: From that first paragraph, does it note anywhere that he, being Ognjenovic, having recently visited the corps command was being given any orders for him to pass down as far as what the brigade would be engaged in?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Had he received orders, it wouldn't say "information" at the top here. He would refer to some order. He would say: "Pursuant to such-and-such an order," whereas this is a pure piece of information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want you to go -- paragraph number 2 at the very, very end before -- right -- immediately before paragraph number 3, this information states: "There will be no retreat when it comes to the Srebrenica enclave. We must advance. The enemy's life has to be made unbearable and their temporary stay in the enclave impossible, so they leave the enclave en masse as soon as possible, realising that they cannot survive there." Do you see that section?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, was there any movement of advancing towards the enclave from the moment this information report -- this information is dated, that is 4 July 1994, and the campaign on the attack of Srebrenica, which was a year later, a year plus two days to be exact?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: If we take into consideration this information and the 18th of April, 1993, when Srebrenica was proclaimed a protected area, movement on the part of the units of the Bratunac Brigade towards Srebrenica did not take place until the beginning of the operation in July 1995. So there was no movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Did you by any chance -- were you given any orders to use your artillery equipment to make the enemy's life unbearable during that period of time? Did Ognjenovic -- did Lieutenant Colonel Ognjenovic give you any such orders?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you carry out any orders on your own?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Were any meetings ever held by Lieutenant Ognjenovic to sort of rally his commanders to try to implement this piece of information in this document?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want you to look at paragraph 13. When you look at paragraph 13 and you look at Lieutenant Colonel Ognjenovic's language in the last paragraph -- in the last section of paragraph number 2, did you notice any inherent contradictions?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And could you please tell us exactly what do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: In point 2 it says that the enemy in Srebrenica and the population in Srebrenica as -- that their lives are being made very difficult. Whereas, in point 13, he prohibits the use of all firearms directed at the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, he says that unauthorised opening of fire is strictly forbidden. That's what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. There's nothing else I would be referring to. This is what it says in the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, do you recall when Colonel Blagojevic took over as the commander of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date, but I do know that after the replacement that turned up precipitously that for our former commander, I know that Commander Blagojevic, Vidoje Blagojevic, a colonel from the Drina Corps took over to take up the command of the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, when he took over, do you ever recall there being any meetings where this information was discussed as a policy to be implemented by the brigade under his command?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could very briefly tell us or compare, perhaps, the differences between Colonel Blagojevic and Lieutenant Colonel Ognjenovic, based on your observations and your experience, having worked under both of their commands.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Those differences are enormous. If I were to set them all out, I would be able to put a lot of negative points on one side. When I say "negative," it would to Ognjenovic, and positive would refer to Mr. Blagojevic. Mr. Ognjenovic only had one basic goal, aim. All he wanted to do was to become a big officer himself. And I think that for people who understand me, I've said enough on that score. Now, when I'm talking about Colonel Blagojevic, on the other hand, he was a man who was an unhappy man, an unfortunate man, who arrived at an unfortunate time, who took up his duties in unfortunate -- at an unfortunate time. Because all these decisions, or rather, all his orders were so clear-cut that we always understood them, and that is the main thing as far as I see it. He was a man who shared everything with us, took part in the operation together with us. But it wasn't up to him, because there were far more responsible people and superior people who ordered us what to do. So all these combat orders reflect best his visions and his opinions with respect to Ognjenovic. So I don't know what I can actually add to that. If you have any specific questions, please ask me; and if I'm able to, I shall answer them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, thank you. I think that answers the question. I just wanted to, by way of example, perhaps solidify the point you had indicated with respect to this document being an information. You indicated that had this been an order, it would reflect where it came from and there might be some sort of number or notation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Take a look at a combat order, the one we received for an attack -- to attack Srebrenica. In the upper right-hand corner, somebody has to refer back to an order and say which order he relies upon. And that does not exist in this particular information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's look at that, and that would be Prosecution Exhibit 406. And I also want to show you another document, Prosecution Exhibit 543.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, as you indicated in that list of exhibits, this document P98 was not tendered by the Prosecution. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That was not tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: If it was not tendered, we are not going to consider it. So is it necessary for you to attack these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, because it has been referred to, on numerous occasions, that Colonel Blagojevic was aware of Ognjenovic's information, although they claim to have been some sort of a policy. And that the attack on Srebrenica was a continuation of that policy, and they're anchoring part of their argument as to the forcible transfer, and Mr. Blagojevic being a member of the joint criminal enterprise in part on this particular document. That's why. I don't want to speak of their Prosecution tactics, but that's my understanding of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. This document is mentioned in the indictment. It also is mentioned and discussed in Mr. Butler's reports and cited as such. I did not ask Mr. Butler to comment on it; I thought it was self-explanatory. That document and others like it that Mr. Butler had cited and mentioned in his report but had not talked about, we offered into evidence a while back. And the Court I think denied our offering those materials into evidence. So this was part of a larger group of documents that we did offer. I think at the time the Court was not aware and I don't think we pointed out that among that big group of documents that Mr. Butler cited, there's some rather significant ones, this and a few others. There are a few others as well that I can point out to the Court, but this does -- Mr. Karnavas does bring up a problem and I think he's absolutely justified in using this document because it is a -- an important document. But the reason it didn't get offered with Mr. Butler is because I didn't ask him about it. But that was the case of several of those documents because there was just too many to ask him about everything. I hate to take us back into time like that with all our documents, but that's the -- that's the story on that. Mr. Nikolic also talked about the document, I'm told.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think since we spent a lot of time on this document, the best way is to have it admitted, no matter as a Prosecution document, or as a Defence document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. I just have to clarify one point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If we could look at these two documents, Prosecution Exhibit 406. Now, this is the document we talked about earlier, that's 5 July 1995, the order for active combat operations. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want you to look at this other document, Prosecution Exhibit 543. And it's dated 2 July 1995. Is there anything in these two documents that would give you the impression that they're related, and if so how?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: As I said a moment ago, for somebody to write and issue an order in writing, he must refer to some other order. And in the order to the Bratunac Brigade of the 2nd of July, 1994, that order is based on a previous order, 0207, and the Drina Corps command Krivaja 95. So on the document of the Drina Corps, on the right it says: "Krivaja 95," and that is also included in the order by the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, which means that he bases his order on the previous order, and this shows you that it is in fact an order that somebody issued and he was just passing it down the line, implementing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And we don't have that in this other -- this information, do we?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Well, there's a big difference, not to have to repeat, between an information and an order. And an order is issued by the brigade commander; an information is compiled, as I said a moment ago, pursuant to the rules and regulations, the deputy commander for morale guidance and religious affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Gavric. I don't have any more -- I'm sorry. I forgot to mention one other point. Now that we've clarified this, did there come a time after the searching of the terrain on July 17 that you talked about, did there come a time when you came across or you were handed another set of prisoners that had been captured?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: You mean that day or over the coming days?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Over the coming days, weeks, months. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you recall how many men we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I think the number would be seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know where they came from or where they were captured?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Could you tell us.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: One morning - I don't know exactly what -- how much time had gone by after the end of those operations in Srebrenica - but I came to the Bratunac Brigade headquarters to take up my duties, and some of the military police told me that Sreten Petrovic had taken prisoner a group in the Alibegovic area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Slow down a bit. Who is Sreten Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Sreten Petrovic was for a time the commander of the 3rd Battalion, but since he was wounded during the Srebrenica operation at Divljakinje 789, that feature, he was in hospital undergoing treatment, and he had recovered, and I think one of his next assignments, when he collected some information, was to collect a group of men up and take those seven men prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But he was with the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes. A very good soldier he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And could you tell us what happened to those men, just ultimately what happened to them.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: All of them are alive and well and living all over the world, which is proof that in the Bratunac Brigade when decisions were made, nothing happened that is being rumoured and talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, just -- you gave us the bottom line, but once they came to the Bratunac Brigade, these prisoners, where did they go?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: On that morning when I received that information, I went into the police building, came across these seven men in a room sitting around without any security guards, and in that group I happened to recognise a young guy who was about -- yes, I'm hurrying again. Yes, as I said, he was 20 to 23 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I could just interrupt you here because we're trying to be as efficient as we can. Where did the men go from the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I personally took those men to the command of the 2nd Romanija in Knezina and they were exchanged there at Isevic hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And I apologise for not going into all of the details. I want to thank you very much. I have no further questions, Mr. Gavric. Now I believe the Prosecution or Mr. Stojanovic, the Prosecution, and the Judges may have some questions. I would appreciate it if you could be as forthright and honest as you have been with me. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Stojanovic, do you have any questions to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, Mr. Gavric. I just have a few questions, Your Honours, with respect to the events in the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gavric, before we go on to what is most important to me, could you help me out once again, and may we take a look at P406 once again. And may I ask for the usher's assistance to give you a copy in the B/C/S language.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Which point are you interested in, paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: May we just take a look at the first page first, please, and the three letters "MAB" written in handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what this abbreviation is.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: It is a mixed artillery brigade, or rather, battery. Mixed artillery battery. M-A-B, MAB.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Am I right in saying that the unit you belonged to within the frameworks of the Bratunac Brigade had the character of being a mixed artillery battery?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: The abbreviation is how it stands, and the mixed should have been the mixed artillery group. Because if you had different calibre weapons included, then that would be a mixed artillery group in principle. But we called it the MAB, M-A-B, that is to say, battery. In certain circles we referred to it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: During your examination-in-chief, you said that together with the auxiliary personnel, that is to say those working the computers, security, and so on, that you had about 80 men. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the rules and regulations of service, does it say that the chief of artillery, for example, as a staff officer should be an advisor to the commander for matters of artillery; whereas the mixed artillery battery or mixed artillery group, whichever you like, has its own commanding officer and that he is the commanding officer commanding that particular unit?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I'm going to try and explain that to you now. The chief of artillery is a professional man. In translation, let me put it this way: It is his duty to make proposals to the brigade commander. Then the brigade commander is duty-bound to study the information contained in the proposal - in this case, my own proposal - and to make the final decision as to whether he adopts my proposal or rejects my proposal and then implements it through an order or not. Whereas, the commanding officer of the mixed group, compared to the chief, the chief makes up part of the command of the brigade. And he has commanding officers, komandirs, of the batteries. So each of these units has its own commanding officer or komandir. So that is establishmentwise what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The commanding officers or the komandirs are in command of each of the units, the battery, the group, the artillery battalion, or the regiment. Whereas the chief of the artillery branch as in arms and services would advise the commander. Am I right there?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right. And when it comes to major operations such as this one, the chief of artillery must be directly superior to his subordinates, that is the commanding officers of the units, et cetera, down the line, down the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In this period, that is 1995, mid-1995, in practice carry out both duties, were you the head of artillery and at the same time, the komandir of this unit, this battery, or group?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Precisely so, yes. Because we were a small brigade. We didn't have enough staff, so that much of this work was on my shoulders, if we are referring to the artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So you were both head of artillery and komandir of the artillery battery?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We no longer need this exhibit. During the examination-in-chief by my colleague, Mr. Karnavas, you spoke of the night of the 14th to 15th of July when at around 0145 hours you arrived in the command of the Zvornik Brigade. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You also confirmed that you had contact with the assistant duty officer?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And this assistant duty officer transmitted to you Obrenovic's message?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And you complied with that order and remained there to be ready in case of need?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: According to the duty officer's statement, Obrenovic was there at the time and he was sleeping upstairs?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would I be correct in saying that practically at that time you were subordinated to Obrenovic, acting on the instructions you received when you set out from the command of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: As soon as I came to report to the brigade command, I was, according to the establishment, subordinate to that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If the assistant duty officer is speaking the truth, Obrenovic at that time was physically present in the brigade command or headquarters?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now ask the usher to assist me and to give both the witness and Their Honours an excerpt from the transcript from the examination of Mr. Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first two pages, Your Honours, are in English, and the other two are an unofficial translation by our own translator of the transcript into B/C/S. I would like this shown to the witness. So most -- this is actually a transcript of the 7th of October, 2003, page 2.697.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gavric, I will ask you to read the 17th line, line 17, in B/C/S. When -- on examination by Mr. Karnavas, Obrenovic replies: "Several questions have been put here, but general speaking yes. That's how it was. I can't recall every detail of Gavric's statement, but I do know that he said on the 14th in the evening he had been there, but this is not possible because on the 14th in the evening I was engaged in combat operations. I could not have come to Zvornik, even had I wanted to, because I was cut off." Sir, if what you are testifying to today is correct and if what the assistant duty officer told you is correct, am I right in saying that what Mr. Obrenovic is saying is simply not true?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: It's hard to say, because I personally did not see the man. So there is a possibility that the assistant duty officer said that Obrenovic was asleep. Or maybe he didn't check. He didn't know he wasn't there. And I cannot assert this, because I did not speak to Obrenovic personally. I only spoke to the assistant duty officer. And I'm only saying what he told me, and I abide by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That was precisely my question. So if what the assistant duty officer said is true, then what Obrenovic is saying is not true. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So both cannot be true at the same time?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: Well, on the 14th we didn't have an opportunity. This was in the early morning. We didn't speak directly. And if the assistant duty officer of the Zvornik Brigade said that, well ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And to remove another dilemma, you said today during the examination-in-chief that you practically didn't know Dragan Obrenovic [sic]?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I don't remember ever having seen him. And when I entered the courtroom, I saw someone sitting here. I assume it's him because I've seen him on television.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So you are quite sure that the person who introduced himself as the assistant duty officer, who said that Obrenovic was there, that he was asleep, and that he had left a message for you, that was not Dragan Jokic?

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: No, it couldn't have been. I assume he is a high-ranking officer. He could not have been the assistant. He could have been a corporal, or rather, an officer, but anyway this was not him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: I'm 1.000 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gavric. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MICO GAVRIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we have about five minutes. Ms. Issa, are you going to start your cross-examination now or we have an early break so that your cross-examination could be intact tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. ISSA
utterances.text: I'm in Your Honours' hands. I think perhaps it might be better to have an early break since there's such little time left. But if Your Honour wishes me to start now, I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Any objections, Mr. Karnavas?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's up to you. I have no objection if they wish to start tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe we could start tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I guess we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, Witness, I'm sorry that we have to keep you here overnight, because we haven't finished the proceedings here. So during your stay in The Hague, do not talk to anybody and do not let anybody talk to you about your testimony. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: at 1.39 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 4th day of May, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.
